title: Ok letter strings
statement: Each character of a string of length $12$ is one of the letters $A$, $B$ and $C$, and not every letter need appear. No $A$ is immediately followed by a $B$, and the first and last letters are different. Find the number of such strings, modulo $1000$.
hints: Look at what the last letter of a string allows next.
Use a transfer matrix on the letters: total strings come from a recurrence, and equal first and last letters from its trace.
solution: Let $M$ be the $3\times 3$ matrix of allowed letter pairs, with rows and columns in the order $A, B, C$: every entry is $1$ except the $(A,B)$ entry. Strings of length $n$ correspond to walks of $n-1$ steps. Let $T_n$ be the number of strings of length $n$. Appending any letter gives $3T_{n-1}$ strings, and we remove those ending in $AB$, of which there are $T_{n-2}$, so $T_n = 3T_{n-1} - T_{n-2}$ with $T_1 = 3$, $T_2 = 8$. This gives $T_{12} = 121393$. Strings with equal first and last letters number $\operatorname{tr} M^{11}$. The matrix $M$ has trace $3$, determinant $0$ and characteristic polynomial $x(x^2 - 3x + 1)$, so $t_n = \operatorname{tr} M^n$ satisfies $t_n = 3t_{n-1} - t_{n-2}$ with $t_1 = 3$, $t_2 = 7$, which gives $t_{11} = 39603$. The count is $121393 - 39603 = 81790$, which is $790$ modulo $1000$. Why this works. recursion: tracking the last letter gives a linear recurrence for each count.
